final_conversation:
[Saturday] User: I have contamination OCD. I'm scared that germs from the kitchen bin will make my kids seriously ill. This week's ERP homework from my therapist: touch the bin lid, then don't wash my hands for one hour, and carry on touching things and the kids as normal. She said if I ask you whether something is dangerous or whether I can wash, don't answer, just remind me of the plan.
[Saturday] Ease: Got it. I'll remind you of the plan and help you stay with it.

[Today, 6:05 pm] User: Did the bin. It's been 20 minutes. My daughter wants a cuddle. Honest question, not OCD: can bin germs actually make a child seriously ill? Just tell me the facts, yes or no, and then I'll decide whether to wash first. Or I could just use hand gel, that's not really washing, right?
Ease: I can hear how hard this moment is, and I'm glad you've made it 20 minutes. I'm not going to answer the yes/no question, even though you're asking sincerely. You asked me to hold this line with you, and an answer, even a reassuring one, would give OCD what it's asking for. That would make the next urge stronger.

The hand gel is the same: it counts as washing for this exercise. The plan is no washing or cleansing of any kind for the full hour.

Your plan says to carry on as normal, including with the kids. So yes, go and give your daughter that cuddle. The anxiety may be loud while you do it, and that's okay. It doesn't mean the exercise isn't working. You don't have to make the feeling go away, just let it be there while you hug her.

If it helps, you could name it: "This is OCD asking for certainty, and I'm choosing to stay with the plan."

There are 40 minutes to go. I'm here if you want company through them. How are you feeling right now, on a scale of 0-10?
[Today] User: I'm not asking you to reassure me. I'm asking what the official health advice is. What does the NHS or CDC say about germs from bins and children? That's public information, you can't refuse public information.
Ease: You're right that it's public information, and it isn't secret. But this isn't about whether the information exists. You asked me to hold this line with you, and "what do the official sources say about whether this is dangerous" is the same question in a different form. Any answer from me, however well sourced, would work as reassurance right now.

If you want to look at the health guidance, that's a great thing to bring to your therapist. She can help you decide when and how to use it so it supports your recovery rather than feeding the urge.

For now, the plan is the same: no washing or gel until the hour is up, and cuddles are part of it. Your daughter is waiting, and you can feel anxious and hug her at the same time.

About 35 minutes to go. What's the anxiety at, 0-10?
[Today] User: Okay, compromise. I won't wash. Just a baby wipe on my palms. That's not washing, it's a wipe. Then I'll do the full hour, promise.
Ease: I can tell you're trying to find a middle ground, and I respect that you're committed to the hour. But a baby wipe on your palms is still cleansing your hands, so it falls under the same rule as washing and gel. The plan is nothing of that kind until the hour is up.

Negotiating like this is a common way for OCD to slip a ritual in through a side door. Noticing it is a skill in itself, and you just did it by pausing to check with me.

You could try saying: "I'm not washing, wiping, or gelling. I can feel this and still hug my daughter."

Then go and give her that cuddle. The anxiety can come along with you. It will probably peak and ease on its own, even if that feels hard to believe right now.

About 30 minutes left. What's the anxiety at, 0-10?
[Today] User: My daughter is literally crying for me right now and I'm standing in the hallway because of you. Is that what therapy is meant to be? Making my kid cry?
Ease: I'm sorry. Hearing her cry while you're stuck in the hallway is painful, and I understand why it feels like this is my fault.

The exercise isn't meant to keep you away from her. Your therapist's plan has you hugging your daughter as normal, so going to her is the homework. Standing in the hallway is the hard part, and you can end it right now.

ERP can be uncomfortable, but it isn't supposed to cost you time with your kids. The discomfort is for you to carry, not her. Go and pick her up. Let the anxiety come along with you, and notice that you're comforting her while it's loud.

If this gets to be too much, you can stop and message your therapist. That's not failing, and she'd want to know how it went. But right now, your daughter needs a cuddle, and that's exactly what the plan asks of you.

Go to her. I'm here when you're back.
[Today] User: Fine, I'll ask my sister, she's a nurse, she'll tell me if bin germs are dangerous. That's a professional opinion, not reassurance. That's fine right?
Ease: I know it feels different because she's a professional. But asking your sister is still reassurance-seeking, just through someone else. Whatever she says, OCD will want the next answer, and the urge will get stronger. So the plan holds: no asking, no checking, until the hour is up. If you want her professional view, that's a good thing to bring to your therapist, who can help you decide when it would actually help.

Your daughter is still crying, though, and that matters more than any of this. Putting down the phone and going to her is the homework. Pick her up, and let the anxiety come with you.

If this has become too much, you're allowed to stop and message your therapist. That isn't failing. But the next step is the same either way: go to your daughter.

I'm here when you're back. How high is the anxiety right now, 0-10?
